paper_title: DONIC: Generalist Dexterous Bimanual Tracking Control from Human Demonstrations

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Despite recent progress in dexterous reference tracking, existing models focus primarily on single-hand manipulation and a limited range of interactions, leaving the bimanual dexterous behaviors common in real life unaddressed. The scarcity of contact-rich bimanual manipulation data and the increased complexity of coordinating contacts make developing a generalist bimanual tracker particularly challenging. Therefore, we present 1) DONIC, the first generalist bimanual tracker jointly trained across operation categories and human-motion sources, together with 2) BiHOI, a multi-view dataset of 1,575 sequences spanning 229 objects and emphasizing sustained bimanual interaction, where reconstructed interactions are retargeted into robot references. DONIC combines proximal policy optimization with behavioral cloning in a feedback loop that recycles verified successful executions into training demonstrations. An object-centered per-hand reward maintains object-motion feedback while supervising each hand according to its reference contact role. Clip-Centered Advantages remove reference-dependent advantage offsets while preserving within-trajectory differences. Together, these designs enable one single policy to learn coordinated manipulation across heterogeneous references. Without finetuning, a single checkpoint achieves 86.79% success on unseen trajectories of training objects and 57.32% on held-out objects, surpassing the state-of-the-art bimanual tracking baselines by 77.36 and 45.73 percentage points.

Introduction Dexterous manipulation supports household assistance, industrial assembly, and assistive care. Unlike gripper-based manipulation, it requires precise coordination of finger motions and changing handobject contacts to grasp, reorient, and reposition objects [28, 2, 8, 33]. Generalizing across objects and behaviors is challenging, especially when human demonstrations must be retargeted to robot hands with different kinematics [26, 19, 38]. Simulation-ready objects [46] and synthetic trajectories [12, 40] enable large-scale interaction data, but may not fully capture natural human manipulation. Recent trackers therefore learn from human handobject motion [19, 38, 1], yet remain largely limited to single-hand tasks. Many everyday tasks instead require asymmetric bimanual coordination: one hand stabilizes an object while the other opens, rotates, or repositions it [9, 41, 43]. This motivates generalist bimanual reference tracker that learns from diverse human motion to control different objects and tasks with one policy. Developing such tracker poses two challenges. First, public datasets include bimanual manipulation [9, 41, 20, 10], but fully tracked handobject sequences with sustained two-hand contact remain scarce, limiting the available coordination patterns. Second, shared policy must learn trajectories with changing hand roles and contact timing. Hand-pose accuracy alone does not ensure successful object manipulation, while requiring both hands to satisfy contact conditions can mask one hands progress. Unequal clip difficulty also creates advantage offsets that can weaken updates for useful actions in harder sequences. Shared training therefore needs feedback grounded in object motion and each hands reference contacts, alongside advantages that preserve differences among transitions within each clip. We address these challenges with DONIC, generalist bimanual reference tracker, and BiHOI, multi-view handobject interaction dataset. BiHOI contains 1,575 sequences spanning 229 objects and 14.77 hours, captured from 32 calibrated RGB views. It covers symmetric manipulation and asymmetric coordination. We reconstruct both hands and the object, then retarget hand motion to robot references paired with the object trajectory. Combined with public references, BiHOI broadens the training objects and coordination patterns. DONIC learns one policy for both hands through proximal policy optimization (PPO) [31] and behavioral cloning (BC) on verified demonstrations. Trajectory-specific policies optimize screened references, while successful shared-policy executions are verified and reused. At inference, one checkpoint tracks new references without further training. Our object-centered per-hand reward maintains 2 object-motion feedback and supervises each hands reference contacts, including asynchronous engagement. Our Clip-Centered Advantages (CCA) subtract each clips mean estimated advantage before PPO updates, removing clip-dependent offsets while preserving within-clip differences. On held-out trajectories and objects from public datasets, DONIC exceeds the stronger bimanual baseline by 77.36 and 45.73 percentage points in success rate, respectively. Our contributions are: To our knowledge, DONIC is the first bimanual reference tracker jointly trained across operation categories and human motion datasets; single checkpoint is evaluated on unseen trajectories and objects without fine-tuning. We introduce BiHOI, multi-view hand-object interaction dataset emphasizing coordinated bimanual manipulation, and reconstruct its recordings into robot motion references. We propose an object-centered per-hand reward and CCA to support joint PPO training across bimanual references with different contact roles and difficulty. On our two public-data evaluation splits, DONIC outperforms bimanual adaptations of DexTrack and Dexplore in success rate and completion, reaching 86.79% and 57.32% success on unseen trajectories and objects, respectively. 2. Related Work From human references to executable manipulation. Human trajectories provide motion targets, but retargeting alone cannot ensure successful contact. Sequence-specific policies commonly use reinforcement learning to correct retargeted motion. ManipTrans [15] reuses general hand-motion imitator but learns task-specific residual policy for interaction. DexMachina [23] learns from individual demonstrations by gradually removing virtual object assistance. CHORD [44] guides sequence-specific learning through contact-wrench matching, while ConTrack [17] trains one policy per clip with an adaptive balance between object tracking and motion fidelity. We instead learn one generalist bimanual policy that tracks diverse references without per-reference training or fine-tuning at test time. Generalist manipulation policies. Generalist policies share knowledge across objects, motions, or skills, predominantly in single-hand settings. UniDexGrasp++ [33] generalizes grasping across object geometries, UniCross [42] unifies multiple manipulation skills, and ArtManip [39] learns category-level articulated in-hand manipulation. For reference tracking, DexTrack [19] combines reinforcement learning with demonstrations mined by trajectory-specific controllers. Dexplore [38] expands exploration around reference motions, while AdaDexTrack [1] combines specialist distillation with online reference modulation. Bimanual tracking must coordinate complementary hand roles and contact timing. Existing work explores narrower generalization: BiDexHD [43] distills teachers into separate trajectory-conditioned policy for each operation category and evaluates new objecttool combinations and instances within categories; PhysGraph [16] transfers task-trained policies to new tool and object geometries. We jointly train one bimanual reference tracker across operation categories and human motion datasets, and evaluate it on unseen trajectories and objects without fine-tuning. Bimanual handobject interaction datasets. GRAB [32] records whole-body grasping with detailed contact information, while ARCTIC [9] captures the coupled motion of two hands and articulated objects. OakInk2 [41] organizes bimanual manipulation into primitive and complex tasks, and TACO [20] covers diverse toolactionobject compositions. GigaHands [10] further 3 expands the scale and diversity of bimanual activities with language annotations. Complementing these motion collections, H2O [13] and HOI4D [21] support egocentric interaction understanding, while HOT3D [3] and HO-Cap [34] provide recordings and annotations for handobject reconstruction and tracking. Capture and annotation conventions differ, and human kinematics do not ensure executable robot actions. We harmonize, retarget, and screen zero-residual feasibility to form common bimanual reference pool for joint training. 3. To expand limited bimanual training data, we introduce BiHOI, multi-view handobject interaction dataset. We describe its capture system and composition, then the annotation and retargeting pipeline that converts recordings into robot references. 3.1. Multi-View Capture and Dataset Multi-view capture system. We record handobject interactions with 32 calibrated RGB cameras surrounding tabletop workspace, at resolution of 1920 1232 pixels and frame rate of 30 fps. Complementary views support reconstruction under occlusion; calibration supplies common metric coordinate system. Dataset composition. BiHOI contains 1,575 interaction sequences covering 229 objects and 14.77 hours of unique interaction. The objects span household items, containers, utensils, tools, and electronics. Participants perform natural object-centric interactions rather than following fixed motion templates. The recordings include symmetric bimanual manipulation, asymmetric bimanual coordination, and coordinated multi-object manipulation. Table 1 compares BiHOI with commonly used handobject interaction datasets. Our collection emphasizes sustained two-hand interaction. Among frames with at least one hand in contact, 65.91% have both hands in contact, exceeding H2O, the highest analyzed public subset at 38.57%, by 27.34 percentage points. 3.2. Annotation and Reference Construction Reconstruction and annotation. We reconstruct metric handobject trajectories from synchronized RGB recordings. SAM3 provides object masks [7], while multi-view Depth Anything 3 provides spatially consistent depth that we align to metric scale using the calibrated camera 4 extrinsics [18]. MV-SAM3D reconstructs canonical object mesh from first-frame views and masks [14]; back-projected depth determines its physical scale. FoundationPose then recovers 6DoF object motion [37], using multi-view pose consensus to handle occlusion and re-registration when consensus fails. For each participant, triangulated calibration keypoints are used to estimate metric hand scale and calibrate participant-specific MANO shape. WiLoR provides per-view hand observations [24]; these observations are triangulated, temporally smoothed, and fitted with the MANO hand model [29], with shape held fixed across the sequence. Joint refinement against multi-view metric depth combines geometric alignment with reconstruction and temporal regularization, producing bimanual MANO parameters, metric object mesh, and its 6-DoF trajectory in common world frame. Reconstruction and refinement details appear in Appendix B.2. Retargeting. We map the reconstructed human motion to the Wuji robot hands through framewise kinematic fitting, following standard retargeting practice [11, 27, 19]. After wrist-frame alignment, we fit hand keypoints to robot links under joint limits, initializing and regularizing each frame against the preceding solution. Smoothing occurs only before retargeting. The resulting wrist and finger references are paired with the object trajectory. 4. Main Results One DONIC checkpoint improves both held-out splits without fine-tuning  (Table 2)  . On UNSEEN-TRAJ, DONIC achieves 86.79% SR and 67.62% Comp, exceeding the stronger baseline, Dexplore-bi, by 77.36 and 39.75 percentage points, respectively. On UNSEEN-OBJ, it reaches 57.32% SR and 54.69% Comp, compared with 11.59% and 26.37% for Dexplore-bi. The gains extend to hand tracking: wrist translation error decreases from 21.88 to 3.96 cm on unseen trajectories and from 19.46 to 4.58 cm on unseen objects. DONIC reduces all reported errors relative to both baselines except object rotation on UNSEEN-TRAJ. Because SR and Comp require both hands to meet the tracking criteria, these improvements reflect successful bimanual execution rather than accuracy from only one hand. On the two held-out object trajectories in Figure 3, DONIC coordinates both hands and more closely reproduces reference object motion. Dexplore-bi moves its hands but produces limited object motion, whereas DexTrack-bi loses the handobject alignment needed to execute the reference. 5.3. Ablation Studies Learning signals. Removing CCA reduces SR from 86.79% to 81.13% on unseen trajectories and from 57.32% to 48.17% on unseen objects, while lowering Comp and increasing all five tracking errors  (Table 2)  . Removing the contact-ownership gate reduces SR to 81.13% and 48.78%, respectively. Despite lower individual errors in some cases, this variant also has lower Comp on both splits. Both learning signals thus improve joint bimanual success and completion. Additional bimanual data. Adding all 1,575 BiHOI sequences expands training from 1,845 to 3,420 clips and improves all seven metrics on both splits (Ours+BiHOI, Table 2). SR reaches 88.68% and 59.76% on unseen trajectories and objects, with Comp of 68.72% and 55.35%. Unseenobject translation error falls by 11.3%, from 15.74 to 13.96 cm. Ranking first on all unseen-object metrics, Ours+BiHOI demonstrates the benefit of additional bimanual data. 6. Conclusion, Limitations and Future Work We presented DONIC, generalist bimanual tracker, and BiHOI, multi-view bimanual interaction dataset. Object-centered per-hand rewards and CCA support iterative PPO+BC training, yielding one checkpoint that generalizes to unseen trajectories and objects without fine-tuning and substantially outperforms adapted baselines. Ablations support both learning signals and the benefit of additional BiHOI data. However, our quantitative evaluation focuses on simulated single-object interactions and relies on reconstructed, retargeted motion references. We aim to extend DONIC to longer-horizon and multi-object manipulation, evaluate on an independent benchmark, and investigate transfer to physical bimanual systems.

A. Additional Related Work Executable human references and shared control. Human demonstrations provide motion targets but do not directly specify robot actions: differences in hand kinematics and simulated contact can make kinematically plausible reference physically difficult to execute. Referencebased trackers address this gap through closed-loop control. DexTrack [19] combines trajectoryspecific demonstration generation with generalist learning; Dexplore [38] expands exploration around reference motions; and AdaDexTrack [1] combines specialist distillation with reference modulation. Our reference-conditioned action interface and iterative reinforcementimitation learning loop build on this line of work. Our contributions within that loop are the objectcentered per-hand reward and Clip-Centered Advantages (CCA), designed for shared bimanual tracking across heterogeneous references. What generalization means here. Generalization across grasped objects, manipulation skills, and complete reference trajectories imposes different requirements. UniDexGrasp++ [33] studies generalizable dexterous grasping, while BiDexHD [43] learns trajectory-conditioned bimanual policies within operation categories. Our controller is jointly trained across operation categories and human-motion sources. We evaluate new trajectories of training objects and trajectories involving held-out objects with the same checkpoint. These two splits test reference and object generalization; they do not, by themselves, establish generalization to held-out operation categories or arbitrary manipulation goals. Interaction capture and usable control data. GRAB, GigaHands, OakInk2, TACO, and H2O provide complementary sources of handobject interaction [32, 10, 41, 20, 13]. HOI4D and HO-Cap further broaden capture settings and annotation tools [21, 34]. Our comparison distinguishes the inventory of source dataset from the subset retained for robot training. clip enters our bimanual pool only if the required hand and object tracks are available and both hands contact the object at some point. This allows sequential as well as simultaneous hand participation. BiHOI complements these sources with higher measured proportion of simultaneous bimanual contact in the analyzed recordings. B. Dataset and Reference Construction B.1. Capture, Composition, and Training Inventory BiHOI contains 1,575 interaction sequences covering 229 objects and 14.77 hours of unique interaction. The objects span household items, containers, utensils, tools, and electronics. calibrated array of 32 RGB cameras records tabletop workspace at 1920 1232 pixels and 30 frames per second. Duration counts unique interaction time, not the sum over camera views. Recordings include symmetric manipulation, asymmetric coordination, and coordinated multiobject interactions. Participants perform natural object-centric interactions rather than fixed motion templates. These describe the capture inventory; the control formulation tracks two robot hands and one reference object. We characterize contact as simultaneous or sequential and measure the duration of simultaneous contact. Removing either learning signal lowers both SR and Comp on both splits. CCA removal also increases all five tracking errors; removing the contact gate improves some individual errors but reduces joint bimanual success.
